output.title: The middle is where the decision lives
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to trust a story before the middle has been checked. The middle is where the real work lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the handoff from demo to daily use. That is also where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For a bounded Bareni decision, I would not start with “Will AI do it?” I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. That is what the free 30-minute diagnostic is for: identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

If you want a practical next step, write down one process you repeat every week and the single measure you would accept as success before you commit. Not a vague improvement, but the checkpoint you would actually use. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
